claims.sentence: The MHRA says domperidone is now contraindicated in confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma because of a risk of severe hypertension.
claims.evidence: Title and text: new contraindication in patients with phaeochromocytoma due to the risk of severe hypertension; applies to confirmed or suspected.

claims.sentence: The MHRA published a Drug Safety Update on 21 July 2026 about domperidone.
claims.evidence: Both searches: Drug Safety Update published 21 July 2026.

claims.sentence: Domperidone is now contraindicated in patients with confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma.
claims.evidence: As above; applies to all domperidone products.

claims.sentence: The reason is a risk of severe hypertension (very high blood pressure).
claims.evidence: Reason stated; the parenthetical gloss is a plain textbook definition.

claims.sentence: The MHRA had received no UK Yellow Card reports of this event.
claims.evidence: 'MHRA has not received any UK Yellow Card reports of this reaction'.

claims.sentence: The MHRA says a recent European review of safety data identified an association between domperidone and episodes of severe hypertension in patients with phaeochromocytoma, after a small number of reports.
claims.evidence: 'A European review of safety data found an association ... based on a small number of reports' (second search: four reports).

claims.sentence: Phaeochromocytoma is a rare tumour of the adrenal gland.
claims.evidence: First search: 'a rare adrenal gland tumour'; second: 'an adrenal tumour'. 'Rare' may be the search tool's gloss; low-risk textbook fact either way.

claims.sentence: As a result, domperidone is now contraindicated in patients with confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma, which means it should not be used in them.
claims.evidence: Contraindication stated; 'prescribers should not start domperidone in these patients'.

claims.sentence: The MHRA tells prescribers that patients with confirmed or suspected phaeochromocytoma who are taking domperidone should have treatment stopped and be switched to an alternative.
claims.evidence: Second search: if already taking it, 'stopping it immediately and switching to an alternative treatment'; first search: PDF says patients should stop. Flag: stop-medicine advice, but attributed to prescribers and a diagnosed-patient group; keep that framing, do not generalise to readers.

claims.sentence: It adds that domperidone can unmask the tumour, so a severe hypertensive episode in someone taking it should prompt consideration of further investigation.
claims.evidence: 'domperidone can unmask a phaeochromocytoma, and a severe hypertensive episode in a patient on domperidone should prompt investigation for one'.

claims.sentence: The MHRA says it has not received any UK Yellow Card reports of severe hypertension with domperidone in patients with phaeochromocytoma, and asks that suspected side effects be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.
Anyone with questions about their own treatment can ask the prescriber or pharmacist.
claims.evidence: Not in the retrieved text; generic signposting, directed at an individual (flagged) but is a route-to-care statement, not an instruction to change treatment. Acceptable as textbook.

dateEvidence: Both searches state the gov.uk Drug Safety Update was published on 21 July 2026 (also appears in the July 2026 Safety Roundup). Page header not read directly.
notes: Brief is sound. The link note says no sentence claims domperidone treats nausea; the 'nausea' symptom tag is therefore an unsupported association - the retrieved text never mentions nausea in this DSU (an older DSU title does). Consider dropping the symptom tag. No doses or 'safe' wording. The stop-and-switch sentence is the only one with individual-treatment impact; it must remain attributed to prescribers.
